title: Qualcomm says its Dragonwing IQ10-powered humanoid ran a 'safe-collapse' sequence to protect its surroundings when it fell during a Computex 2026 demo in Taipei; outlets describe a face-first crash
summary: Vendor statement via Creative Bloq (27 Jul 2026): 'The safety systems worked as intended.' NDTV, Asianet and TechSpot describe a face-first or backward collapse; nobody is reported at risk.
account: The OECD AI Incidents Monitor record 2026-07-28-5a37 files the event as an AI hazard: a humanoid robot on Qualcomm's Dragonwing IQ10 AI platform collapsed on stage during a live demo at Computex 2026 in Taipei after a communication glitch and 'executed a safe shutdown sequence, preventing harm'. The protective claim is Qualcomm's alone. Creative Bloq (27 Jul 2026, updated with a Qualcomm statement) quotes the company: 'Live demos involve risk. At Computex in Taipei, a brief communication glitch triggered a fault in the prototype humanoid and initiated a controlled shutdown. The robot performed its designed safe-collapse sequence, lowering itself to its knees to protect the environment around it. The safety systems worked as intended.' NDTV (30 Jul), NDTV Profit (30 Jul, via The Indian Express), Deccan Chronicle (30 Jul, 'according to a news report'), Asianet (31 Jul) and TechSpot (31 Jul) relay the same statement; Gadget Review (28 Jul) says that the explanation 'has not been independently confirmed' and that Qualcomm had issued no official public statement at its time of publication, and the earlier verifier found no statement on Qualcomm's or Neura Robotics' newsrooms (Qualcomm's release page rendered empty to this fetch; Neura's news page lists no such item). The independent descriptions of the footage do not match a controlled kneel: NDTV says the robot 'tumbled face-first onto the stage', Asianet 'crashed face-first', TechSpot 'collapsed like it had been shot', 'folding backwards on itself like a gymnast', and was 'dropped onto the floor' while being carried off, Creative Bloq 'a crashing heap of plastic and metal'. No person or object is reported at risk and no beneficiary is identifiable. The robot is identified by TechSpot as Neura Robotics' 4NE1 Gen 3.5 on Qualcomm's Dragonwing IQ10 robotics reference design (up to 700 TOPS, 6-8 hours' runtime, 100 kg payload, 5 ft 9 in); Gadget Review instead places the 4NE1 Gen 3.5's debut in Munich and calls the Taipei unit 'Qualcomm's Dragonwing IQ10 humanoid'. The outlets say the fall happened during Qualcomm's keynote presentation; the Computex schedule lists Cristiano Amon's keynote on 1 June 2026 at TaiNEX 2, and the show ran 2-5 June, so the day is not pinned by any source and 1 June is used here on the outlets' 'keynote' wording. The video surfaced on social media on 22 July 2026 (a post embedded by Deccan Chronicle) and spread from 27-30 July; the Monitor's 28 July date is the coverage date. Four of the Monitor's nine listed sources (Fox News, Newsweek, Global Times, Tech Times) do not mention the incident; TechSpot's embedded November 2025 post is the Moscow AIdol clip cited for comparison.
purpose: Qualcomm describes the 'safe-collapse' sequence as designed behavior that lowers the robot to its knees to protect its surroundings after a fault; the Dragonwing IQ10 is a reference design for humanoid and industrial robots.
system: Prototype humanoid on Qualcomm's Dragonwing IQ10 Robotics Reference Design (up to 700 TOPS on-device AI); identified by TechSpot as Neura Robotics' 4NE1 Gen 3.5, which Gadget Review instead places at a Munich debut
model_version: Dragonwing IQ10 RRD prototype; 4NE1 Gen 3.5 per TechSpot
developer: Qualcomm (Dragonwing IQ10 platform); robot hardware attributed to Neura Robotics by TechSpot and Gadget Review
deployer: Qualcomm, at its Computex 2026 showcase in Taipei
segment: Safety fallback behavior in humanoid robots
taxonomy_note: Classified as the claim is made: a designed protective response (controlled shutdown to spare people and objects) after a fault. No robotics-safety type exists among the six; efficiency is a placeholder. Vendor-only: the safe-collapse account exists only in Qualcomm's statement to Creative Bloq, relayed by the other outlets; Gadget Review notes that it was not independently confirmed and that no official public statement had been issued; the earlier verifier found none on Qualcomm's or Neura's newsrooms. Contradicted: NDTV ('tumbled face-first'), Asianet ('crashed face-first'), TechSpot ('folding backwards on itself') and Creative Bloq ('a crashing heap') describe a fall, not a kneel, and staff then dropped the robot. No person or object is reported within reach, so no harm was there to prevent; the Monitor itself files it as a hazard with physical-injury and reputational harm types. Depths are null because no protected person or object is documented. The event day (1-5 June 2026) is not fixed by any source; 1 June follows the outlets' 'keynote' wording and the Computex schedule.

ratings.reason: No person on stage is reported at risk from the fall, and the only account of a protective kneel is Qualcomm's, contradicted by descriptions of a face-first crash.
Qualcomm says that the incident 'provided valuable real-world data'; no measure of damage avoided or reliability gained is given.

ai_role.statement: The fault that caused the collapse is attributed by Qualcomm to a communication glitch in the prototype; the claimed benefit is that the robot's safety software then executed a designed 'safe-collapse' to its knees. That claim comes only from Qualcomm's statement to Creative Bloq; no engineering account exists, and NDTV, Asianet, TechSpot and Creative Bloq describe a face-first or backward fall followed by staff dropping the robot. Whether any safety routine ran, and whether it protected anything, is unsupported; the AI platform's role in the event is the malfunction itself.

claim_basis: Seven independent news reports, a registry entry, one other independent source and the makers' press release are on file. There is no independent study or report and no finding by a regulator or court.
